pl-l2d17c5-d1e108.summary: States that paradise is understood as a bodily place in which man was placed.

pl-l2d17c5-d1e111.summary: Distinguishes three views: bodily only, spiritual only, or both; Lombard prefers the third. Man was placed in a bodily paradise, planted from the beginning when the earth brought forth plants; though a type of the Church, it is literally a most pleasant place with fruit trees and a great spring. The old translation's 'to the east' leads some to place it in the east, far from inhabited lands and so high it reached the lunar circle, so the flood did not reach it.
claims: Lombard prefers paradise as both literal and figurative.
Some place paradise high in the east.

pl-l2d17c5.summary: Holds that paradise is understood as a bodily place. Of three views, bodily only, spiritual only, or both, Lombard prefers the third: man was placed in a bodily paradise, planted 'from the beginning' when the earth produced plants, which, though a type of the present or future Church, is literally a most pleasant place, rich in fruit trees and watered by a great spring; the old translation's 'to the east' leads some to place it in the east, far removed from inhabited regions and so high that the flood did not reach it.
claims: Paradise was a real bodily place.
Lombard prefers the view that paradise is both bodily and spiritual.
Paradise is a type of the present or future Church.
Some place paradise in the east, high and remote, untouched by the flood.
